title: MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Mao-xun Huang, Jerry Wang, Yi-Cheng Lai, Zhengxin Zhang, Claire Cardie, Hen-Hsen Huang
abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through task decomposition, agent specialization, information exchange, and intermediate validation. However, existing systems typically treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target. We introduce MANTA, a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures to self-evolve at inference time. Before execution, MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget. We evaluate MANTA against representative single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft. These results show that inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself.

infographic.key_insight: MANTA lets a multi-agent system adapt its communication topology during inference, so the collaboration structure can self-evolve when the current setup is no longer effective.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is relevant for building more robust agentic systems because it suggests topology, not just prompts or policies, can be adjusted online to improve task performance without changing the agent budget.
method: Initialize a task-conditioned network topology from prior structural experience.
Monitor collaboration traces during execution and trigger bounded structural updates when needed.
Adapt roles, links, execution order, visibility, and validation paths while preserving the task interface.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning, MANTA achieved a 74.0 average score and beat the strongest baseline by 5.8 points, with the best result on PlanCraft.
infographic.watch_item: Because the method changes communication structure online, its stability, overhead, and failure modes under noisy traces or tight latency constraints need careful implementation and evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems

title: Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration
authors: Ting Gong, Michael Ruofan Zeng, Yong Yang
abstract: Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management. We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

infographic.key_insight: Albilich is a steerable, agentic framework that coordinates LLM reasoning, CAS, literature retrieval, and persistent state to make long-horizon mathematical research more reproducible and effective.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper shows how adding orchestration, verification, and memory layers can turn a general LLM into a practical research system for theorem proving and open-problem exploration.
method: Long-horizon proof-state management with persistent SQLite context
Advisor/verifier agents plus literature retrieval to steer and check proofs
CAS integration to reduce token use and improve symbolic reasoning
infographic.evidence_signal: On RealMath, Albilich solved 10/10 problems with CAS and 9/10 without CAS, and on Kourovka problems it produced a counterexample and a strengthened proof result.
infographic.watch_item: Results are benchmark- and problem-dependent, and the system’s reliability may hinge on verifier quality, advisor guidance, and careful CAS orchestration.
infographic.paper_title: Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration

title: Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning
authors: Qiangqiang He, Zhongheng Wu, ZiJian Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Token-level shifts from privileged self-distillation are driven more by counterfactual sensitivity than by true answer-aligned learning value, so credit should be reallocated away from highly sensitive tokens.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CSCR is a simple drop-in modification to GRPO that preserves verifier-determined direction while improving long-CoT reasoning performance on mathematical benchmarks.
method: Re-score each sampled trajectory under two counterfactual outcomes: correct vs. incorrect.
Measure which tokens change most and downweight highly sensitive, easily substitutable tokens.
Renormalize token-level advantages to keep the original credit budget and update direction.
infographic.evidence_signal: On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently beats the GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates, and ablations show moderate downweighting works best.
infographic.watch_item: Over-modulating token credit can destabilize optimization, so the sensitivity downweighting must be kept moderate.
infographic.paper_title: Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning

title: ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning
authors: Zhenrong Zhang, Fei Wu, Jun Du, Jianshu Zhang, Si Wei
abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

infographic.key_insight: ReDiPPO improves mathematical reasoning by using reference answers to calibrate value estimates and by reweighting token-level advantages where the standard critic disagrees most with the reference-guided critic.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets a core RL bottleneck for long-horizon reasoning: noisy token credit assignment under sparse rewards, which can improve training stability and final model accuracy.
method: Reference-guided critic uses training-time answer references to produce more accurate value estimates.
Standard critic remains in place, and its discrepancy from the reference-guided critic marks difficult reasoning states.
Token-level advantages are reweighted during PPO updates based on this discrepancy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks, where ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and outperforms PPO, DAPO, and GSPO in final reasoning performance.
infographic.watch_item: Because the approach relies on reference answers during training, performance may depend on access to high-quality supervision and careful handling of train-test mismatch.
infographic.paper_title: ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning

title: $β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation
authors: Jiawei Xu, Minghui Liu, Juzheng Zhang, Tom Goldstein, Furong Huang
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

infographic.key_insight: β-OPSD generalizes vanilla OPSD by treating the KL anchor as a tunable β regularizer, yielding an optimal policy that geometrically interpolates between a reference policy and a privileged teacher.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It preserves the practical efficiency of self-distillation while making optimization more stable and controllable for reasoning-model training.
method: Recast OPSD as a policy-optimization family with β weighting the KL penalty to the reference policy.
Derive a closed-form optimal policy as a geometric mix of reference and teacher distributions.
Approximate the expensive RL objective by distilling token-level logits along the β-selected path, with return-to-go credit assignment.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks showing β-OPSD consistently improves optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance over vanilla OPSD.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on correctly tuning β and implementing the token-level logit mixing/return-to-go alignment without introducing training instability.
infographic.paper_title: $β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation

title: OptGraph: Large Language Models Enhanced Evolutionary Optimization Via Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Xianchao Xiu, Jianhao Li, Huangyue Chen, Wanquan Liu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a powerful tool for automated evolutionary optimization, but existing methods remain limited in pattern reuse, error-aware refinement, and retrieval robustness across diverse tasks. To address these limitations, we propose OptGraph, the first optimization agentic workflow that introduces graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG). Specifically, OptGraph first constructs reusable experience as a typed graph, capturing the relationships among modeling patterns, problem formalization, implementation details, and error corrections. In the inference stage, OptGraph leverages graph neighborhood information to enrich retrieved knowledge, providing structured context to improve modeling, verification, and iterative refinement. Moreover, OptGraph supports adaptive knowledge updates, enabling the distillation of execution traces and verification feedback into reusable graph knowledge without ndertaking LLM parameter tuning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that our proposed OptGraph achieves an average exact accuracy 8.9% higher than the state-of-the-art prompt-based automated optimization frameworks. Our code has been made available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/OptGraph.

infographic.key_insight: OptGraph turns past optimization experience into a typed graph so an LLM can retrieve structured, error-aware context for better evolutionary optimization and refinement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach improves automated modeling and verification without parameter tuning, making it attractive for reusable optimization pipelines in scientific and engineering workflows.
method: Builds a typed graph of reusable experience linking modeling patterns, formalization, implementations, and error fixes.
Retrieves graph neighborhoods at inference to enrich context for generation, verification, and iterative refinement.
Updates the knowledge graph from execution traces and verification feedback without LLM fine-tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: On benchmark datasets, OptGraph reports an average exact accuracy 8.9% higher than state-of-the-art prompt-based automated optimization frameworks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality of graph construction and retrieval, so noisy or incomplete traces could limit robustness.
infographic.paper_title: OptGraph: Large Language Models Enhanced Evolutionary Optimization Via Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

title: Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold
authors: Songshuo Lu, Zhi Chen, Yaohua Tang
abstract: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

infographic.key_insight: A single RL-trained model is treated as a local probe of a larger reasoning manifold, so better students come from constructing and compressing a complementary union of teachers rather than choosing one best teacher.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical recipe for boosting small-model reasoning quality while keeping single-model inference, which is useful for deployable math, code, and instruction-following systems.
method: RGRPO expands coverage by training multiple teachers from one initialization and steering later rounds toward uncovered examples.
TU-OPD compresses the teacher union into a student using reliability-gated, on-policy distillation from the student’s own response prefixes.
Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves a winner teacher’s extra token preferences so specialist behaviors are not averaged away.
infographic.evidence_signal: On math reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, the Qwen3-1.7B student beat the strongest individual teacher with reported relative gains of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%.
infographic.watch_item: The approach adds training complexity and depends on reliable teacher selection/quality scoring, which may be sensitive to implementation details and domain coverage.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold

title: LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts
authors: Ken Ding
abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

infographic.key_insight: LSPO fixes a zero-gradient failure mode in RLVR by temporarily adding a low-rank LoRA scaffold to regenerate learning signal on "cliff" prompts where GRPO would otherwise get none.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical training-time patch for improving mathematical reasoning models without changing the final deployment model, since the adapter is used only during sampling and discarded afterward.
method: Detect prompts where all group rollouts fail and the RL advantage collapses to zero.
Fit a small LoRA adapter on ground-truth solutions for those cliff prompts.
Re-roll with base+adapter, importance-correct the successful samples, and update the base model with GRPO.
infographic.evidence_signal: On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, LSPO matched or beat a DAPO baseline on all 16 benchmark/pass@k cells across 5 paired seeds, with an average +3.8-point gain and up to +10.7 on AIME24/pass@4.
infographic.watch_item: The extra supervised scaffold step and importance-sampling splice add training complexity and may be sensitive to how cliff prompts are detected, how the adapter is fit, and whether the correction remains stable.
infographic.paper_title: LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts

title: Neural Network Approximation of Solutions to Fractional Parabolic Partial Differential Equations
authors: Jae-Hwan Choi, Hyojae Lim, Jinsol Seo, Young-Jin Sim, Changhoon Song
abstract: We establish a dimension-efficient neural network approximation theory for solutions to fractional parabolic equations with lower-order drift and potential terms. By introducing anisotropic spectral Barron spaces, which measure temporal and spatial regularity separately in frequency space, we first develop a dimension-independent maximal regularity theory for these equations, using dimension-independent multiplication estimates and the method of continuity to incorporate the lower-order terms. A key technical novelty is the application of the Vandermonde matrix to the global-in-time extension of the finite-time fractional heat semigroup with sufficient regularity at the initial time, thereby enabling analysis of the forward-in-time evolution via the global space-time Fourier structure of anisotropic Barron norms. We also show that a corresponding uniform-in-time estimate of the spectral Barron regularity generally fails. Finally, we derive $n^{-1/2}$ two-layer approximation bounds in mixed Sobolev norms for non-constant periodic activations and, under additional anisotropic Barron regularity, for non-periodic activations satisfying a polynomial-decay condition.

infographic.key_insight: The paper develops a dimension-independent theory showing that fractional parabolic PDE solutions can be efficiently approximated by neural networks using anisotropic spectral Barron spaces that separate time and space regularity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a theoretical foundation for scalable neural solvers for high-dimensional fractional diffusion models with drift and potential terms, with provable approximation rates.
method: Introduce anisotropic spectral Barron spaces to measure temporal and spatial frequency regularity separately.
Prove dimension-independent maximal regularity using multiplication estimates and the method of continuity.
Use a Vandermonde-based global-in-time extension of the fractional heat semigroup to analyze forward evolution in space-time Fourier variables.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical approximation guarantees, including n^{-1/2} two-layer network bounds in mixed Sobolev norms under specified activation and regularity conditions.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest guarantees depend on anisotropic Barron regularity assumptions, and uniform-in-time spectral Barron regularity can fail in general.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Network Approximation of Solutions to Fractional Parabolic Partial Differential Equations

title: Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioners for Iterative Solvers
authors: Zechen Zhang, Rui Peng Li, Yousef Saad
abstract: Solving large, sparse linear systems is a core task in scientific computing, and efficient iterative solvers rely critically on effective and robust preconditioning. While classical methods such as algebraic multigrid (AMG) are highly scalable, their robustness can degrade on indefinite or nonsymmetric systems where heuristics originally developed for elliptic PDEs are less reliable. Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as data-driven preconditioners; yet, the practical impact of imposing an AMG-style hierarchy remains underexplored for general sparse matrices. In this work, we propose a Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioner (GMP) that adopts an AMG hierarchy as a structural prior and learns smoothing, restriction, and interpolation operators in a unified framework. Our method targets general sparse systems and is instantiated as a drop-in preconditioner for standard Krylov solvers. On a benchmark of over 800 sparse matrices, we compare against classical AMG, single-level ILUT, and state-of-the-art GNN preconditioners, and characterize the regimes where multilevel graph neural preconditioning improves convergence or, conversely, introduces overhead relative to strong single-level baselines. These results highlight both the promise and the limitations of enforcing AMG-style multilevel structure in learned preconditioners for large-scale scientific simulations.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that a graph neural network can be used as a multilevel preconditioner by combining an AMG-style hierarchy with learned smoothing, restriction, and interpolation operators for sparse linear systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could improve Krylov solver performance on large scientific computing problems, especially where classical AMG is less robust for indefinite or nonsymmetric matrices.
method: Uses an algebraic multigrid-like multilevel structure as a prior
Learns smoothing, restriction, and interpolation in a unified GNN framework
Wraps the result as a drop-in preconditioner for standard Krylov solvers
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluate the method on more than 800 sparse matrices and compare it against classical AMG, ILUT, and recent GNN preconditioners.
infographic.watch_item: The multilevel learned design may add overhead and does not guarantee improvement over strong single-level baselines in all regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioners for Iterative Solvers

title: On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces
authors: Imad Aouali
abstract: This thesis studies policy learning in interactive systems where an agent observes a context, selects an action from a very large set, and receives partial feedback. The main framework is contextual bandits, with two paradigms: on-policy learning, where the agent interacts sequentially with the environment and minimizes regret, and off-policy learning, where it learns from logged data collected by a logging policy. In large action spaces, both settings face major challenges: inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. The first part develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy learning. We introduce meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and dTS, which leverages diffusion-inspired priors to model dependencies between actions. These methods share information across actions and yield regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions. The second part addresses off-policy learning. We propose sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, show that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, and introduce concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Finally, we develop differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

infographic.key_insight: The thesis shows that in large action spaces, policy learning becomes tractable when actions are tied together through structured priors or latent representations, rather than treating every action independently.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for recommendation, ranking, and decision systems with many actions because it offers scalable ways to learn from sparse feedback while controlling regret, bias, and variance.
method: meTS: a mixed-effect Thompson sampling method that shares statistical strength across actions.
dTS: a diffusion-inspired structured prior that captures similarity among actions for better exploration.
Off-policy learning: latent-variable structured direct methods plus concave policy-weighted objectives and pessimistic smoothing to stabilize importance-sampling estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports regret guarantees for the on-policy methods and optimization-vs-estimation analyses, plus PAC-Bayesian control of the bias-variance trade-off for the off-policy estimators.
infographic.watch_item: These methods rely on structured assumptions and careful optimization, so performance may degrade if the action dependencies or logging-policy coverage are misspecified.
infographic.paper_title: On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces

title: When Do Learned Diffusion Proposals Help Constraint Solving? A Controlled Study on Continuous Algebraic Systems
authors: Quang Bui, Sparsh Roy, Akash Gundimeda, Davin Yin
abstract: Solving a continuous algebraic constraint system requires two decisions: which values satisfy the constraints, and which structural augmentation renders an unsolvable system solvable. Classical solvers answer the first well and the second only by enumeration. On that discrete decision, a candidate-conditioned repair ranker choosing among K augmentations reaches the exhaustive-search ceiling at a fraction of the calls, outperforming random (0.997 vs 0.236 balanced nonlinear menu accuracy; p < 10^-70; 0.982 +/- 0.006 across seeds) and beating a budget-matched per-candidate probe on accuracy and cost. MARC turns such a system into a factor graph, over which a graph-neural diffusion denoiser proposes assignments, descent on an exact computer-algebra energy polishes them, and an exact symbolic checker certifies solutions. Evaluations of diffusion-based proposals rarely include one control: random multi-start under the same refinement budget. Applied to our system, it sharply curtails what the learned proposal contributes on the value decision. Does it beat random multi-start at choosing satisfying assignments? Only narrowly, in a predictable regime. Across trapped low-dimensional families it ties with random restart, but dominates in high dimension, where random search fails. Once variables couple, the advantage is gone. Since all methods share one polish and one checker, best-of-K random multi-start succeeds with probability exactly 1 - (1 - q(n))^K, where q(n) is single-start reachability; one measured constant, with no free parameters, reproduces the entire curve (mean absolute error 0.012). The favorable regime is not specific to our synthetic families: across eight real-world systems in robotics, positioning, optimization, and algebra, classical multi-start solved all eight, none in the learning-favorable regime. We map the regimes in which learned proposals improve solvers.

infographic.key_insight: Learned diffusion proposals help continuous constraint solving only in narrow regimes; for many systems, budget-matched random multi-start is just as good or better once exact polishing and checking are included.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solver design, the main gain from learning may lie in discrete repair/augmentation selection, while value assignment often remains competitive with simpler randomized search under the same compute budget.
method: Model the constraint problem as a factor graph and use a graph-neural diffusion denoiser to propose continuous assignments.
Polish each proposal with descent on an exact computer-algebra energy, then certify with an exact symbolic checker.
Compare against matched random multi-start baselines and a candidate-conditioned repair ranker over the same refinement budget.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that random multi-start matches learned proposals in trapped low-dimensional cases, dominates in high dimension, and that a simple best-of-K formula accurately predicts success across curves with mean absolute error 0.012.
infographic.watch_item: The learned advantage appears regime-dependent and can disappear when variables are strongly coupled, so evaluation must include a strict random-restart control under identical polishing and checking budgets.
infographic.paper_title: When Do Learned Diffusion Proposals Help Constraint Solving? A Controlled Study on Continuous Algebraic Systems

title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning for Small-Scale Language Model Agents
authors: Md Rezwanul Haque, Md. Milon Islam, Fakhri Karray
abstract: The alignment of Small Language Models (SLMs) in the 70--500M parameter range using reinforcement learning is often considered unstable, though the underlying failure mechanisms have not been systematically investigated. In the State-of-the-Art (SOTA) research, fifteen (model, corpus) configurations were trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The experiments included Pythia-70M, 160M, 410M and SmolLM2-135M, 360M on the TinyStories, CNN/DailyMail, and Wikitext-103 corpora. Three reproducible failure modes were identified in small-scale language models: silent LoRA parameter freezing in standard PEFT/TRL pipelines, numerical overflow in importance ratios when using bfloat16, and catastrophic policy collapse due to reward-model error. These issues were addressed using a merge-and-reinitialize adapter technique, float32 precision during PPO updates, and a three-layer safety mechanism comprising reward whitening, importance-ratio guarding, and weight rollback. In this paper, a capacity-headroom hypothesis is proposed, which states that PPO performance at the SLM scale depends on both a fluent supervised model ($\text{PPL}<20$) and a discriminative reward signal, rather than on the number of model parameters. The proposed system converged stably in all experiments and improved preference win rate over the SFT baseline in configurations with a fluent prior and an informative reward signal. Furthermore, it outperformed instruction-tuned baselines while requiring significantly less training data. All checkpoints, preference datasets, and training scripts are publicly released$^§$.

infographic.key_insight: Robust PPO for small language model agents depends more on having a fluent supervised prior and a reliable reward signal than on raw parameter count.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper provides practical fixes for unstable RLHF-style training in small models, including adapter reinitialization, float32 PPO updates, and rollback safeguards.
method: Train SLMs with PPO across multiple model/corpus pairs.
Fix silent PEFT/TRL LoRA freezing via merge-and-reinitialize adapters.
Stabilize optimization with float32 updates plus reward whitening, ratio guarding, and rollback.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 15 model–corpus configurations, the proposed safeguards produced stable convergence and improved preference win rate over SFT, with stronger gains when the prior was fluent and the reward signal was informative.
infographic.watch_item: The method still depends on a sufficiently good reward model; if reward quality is weak, policy collapse can still occur despite the safeguards.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning for Small-Scale Language Model Agents

title: ReCo: Reweighting GRPO Against Distributional Concentration
authors: Junoh Park, Junseo Hwang, Wonguk Cho, Taesup Kim
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has become a standard reinforcement learning method for post-training language models. Recent work shows that GRPO can reduce the base model's reasoning capacity and underperform it in Pass@k when k is large, indicating reduced coverage of reasoning paths. We find that this reduction is associated with GRPO concentrating on responses that the base model already generates with high probability. We trace this concentration to two mechanisms in the GRPO update. At the response level, high-probability responses dominate the group gradient through repeated occurrence. At the token level, GRPO's importance ratio scales gradients, further reinforcing tokens that become more likely under the current policy. We propose ReCo, a reweighting method that addresses both effects. Response contributions are normalized by their expected occurrence within the rollout group, and the token-level importance ratio is replaced with a variance-based ratio that gives larger update scale to non-saturated decision points where alternative token choices remain plausible. Across Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ReCo improves Pass@k for large values of k and is comparable to GRPO for small values of k.

infographic.key_insight: GRPO can hurt reasoning diversity by overemphasizing high-probability responses and saturated token choices, and ReCo fixes this with reweighting at both the response and token levels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For post-training math LMs, ReCo offers a practical way to preserve exploration and improve large-k Pass@k without sacrificing small-k performance.
method: Normalize each response's contribution by its expected occurrence in the rollout group.
Replace the standard token-level importance ratio with a variance-based ratio.
Amplify updates at non-saturated decision points where alternative tokens are still plausible.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on five math reasoning benchmarks, ReCo improves Pass@k for large k and remains comparable to GRPO for small k.
infographic.watch_item: The reweighting scheme adds design complexity and may require careful tuning to avoid instability or unintended shifts in update scale.
infographic.paper_title: ReCo: Reweighting GRPO Against Distributional Concentration

title: Large Language Model for Operations Research Formulation Selection in Multi-Warehouse Inventory Allocation
authors: Jintao Xu, Yingzheng Ma, Jiong Dong, Yongzhi Qi, Jianshen Zhang
abstract: Multi-warehouse inventory allocation is typically formulated as a mixed-integer programming (MIP) problem, yet no single formulation consistently matches heterogeneous instance-level regimes induced by demand concentration, inventory imbalance, replenishment scale, service constraints, and forecast volatility. We study this issue as instance-wise operations research (OR) formulation selection, where each allocation instance is assigned to a solver-executable formulation from a candidate OR expert library. We propose a solver-guided large language model (LLM) framework for OR formulation selection, in which each OR expert corresponds to a MIP formulation encoding a distinct allocation priority. To train the selector, the framework first constructs balanced expert-conditioned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) records for schema learning, and then uses MIP solver evaluation on historical instances to convert solver-evaluated allocation-quality gaps into margin-weighted identity preference optimization (IPO) preferences and per-instance expert-score metadata for reward lookup during group relative policy optimization (GRPO) to assign rewards to sampled responses. Experiments on multi-warehouse inventory allocation instances from JD$\mathord{.}$com, one of China's largest e-retailers, demonstrate that GRPO substantially improves expert-selection accuracy relative to the SFT+IPO selector and, more importantly, produces higher realized allocation quality than both the preference-trained selector and the best fixed formulation. With GRPO, Hit Ratio@1 and Hit Ratio@2 increase from 21.45% to 50.42% and from 70.47% to 82.31%. The resulting selector achieves an allocation accuracy gain of 12.57 percentage points over the incumbent baseline, outperforming both the SFT+IPO selector and the best fixed OR expert, and reduces the gap to the ex-post oracle to 4.85 percentage points.

infographic.key_insight: A solver-guided LLM can choose the best mixed-integer programming formulation for each multi-warehouse inventory instance, improving allocation quality beyond any single fixed formulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This turns OR model selection into an instance-wise decision problem, helping e-commerce planning systems adapt formulations to changing demand, inventory, and service regimes.
method: Build a candidate library of solver-executable MIP formulations, each encoding a different allocation priority.
Create balanced supervised fine-tuning data for schema learning, then derive margin-weighted preference data from solver-evaluated quality gaps.
Train the selector with IPO and GRPO, using per-instance expert-score metadata as reward lookup during policy optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: On JD.com inventory allocation instances, GRPO raised Hit Ratio@1 from 21.45% to 50.42% and Hit Ratio@2 from 70.47% to 82.31%, and improved allocation accuracy by 12.57 percentage points over the incumbent baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and coverage of the expert library and solver-labeled historical instances, so deployment may be sensitive to domain shift and the cost of generating preference data.
infographic.paper_title: Large Language Model for Operations Research Formulation Selection in Multi-Warehouse Inventory Allocation

title: SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute
authors: Hongyu Chen, Liang Lin, Guangrun Wang
abstract: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

infographic.key_insight: SVR learns to self-verify its own answers and use that signal to stop early when confident, reducing test-time compute without relying on external feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical adaptive inference strategy for reasoning systems, letting harder inputs get more refinement while easy inputs finish with fewer turns.
method: Multi-turn reinforcement learning with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories
Each turn predicts a solution plus a discrete verdict and confidence score
Retain the answer only if verdict = Correct and confidence clears a threshold; otherwise continue refinement
infographic.evidence_signal: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR reports 0.563 macro-average accuracy with 2.99 inference turns on average.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on well-calibrated self-verification and thresholding, so miscalibration could cause premature stopping or unnecessary extra compute.
infographic.paper_title: SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute

title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules
authors: Jiaxiang Li, Zhiqi Bu, Shiyun Xu
abstract: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that training loss depends jointly on learning-rate and batch-size schedules, and derives a closed-form optimal batch-size schedule for any chosen learning-rate schedule.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical recipe for dynamic batch-size scheduling that can improve large-model training efficiency beyond static batch-size baselines.
method: Model training dynamics using a convex-optimization lens.
Derive a joint loss characterization in terms of learning-rate and batch-size schedules.
Use this characterization to obtain closed-form optimal batch-size schedules and joint scaling laws.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the proposed joint scaling laws consistently outperform static batch-size baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The closed-form schedule still needs careful integration with real training systems, since optimizer, hardware, and memory constraints may limit how freely batch size can vary.
infographic.paper_title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules

title: TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning
authors: Md Joshem Uddin, Astrit Tola, Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora, Baris Coskunuzer
abstract: We introduce Topoformer, a lightweight and scalable framework for graph representation learning that encodes topological structure into attention-friendly sequences. At the core of our method is Topo-Scan, a novel module that decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture multi-scale structural patterns, from local motifs to global organization, and are processed by a Transformer to produce expressive graph-level embeddings. Unlike traditional persistent homology pipelines, Topo-Scan is parallelizable, avoids costly diagram computations, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of our topological encodings and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. Our results show that Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

infographic.key_insight: TopoFormer turns graph topology into short token sequences via Topo-Scan, letting a Transformer learn from multi-scale structural patterns without expensive persistent-homology diagrams.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a parallelizable, lightweight way to inject topological inductive bias into scalable graph learning pipelines for classification and molecular prediction.
method: Slice graphs with node/edge filtrations to create ordered topological tokens.
Feed the resulting sequence into a Transformer for graph-level embeddings.
Use a stability-guaranteed topological encoding that avoids costly diagram computation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art results on graph classification and molecular property prediction, outperforming or matching strong GNN and topology-based baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on how well Topo-Scan discretizes topology into short sequences, so filtration design and token length may affect expressiveness and compute.
infographic.paper_title: TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning

title: Formally certifying number field invariants
authors: Alain Chavarri Villarello, Sander R. Dahmen
abstract: Number fields, which generalize the rational numbers, are fundamental objects in number theory. Many of their key arithmetic properties are captured by invariants whose computation is among the central tasks of computational algebraic number theory and a focus of several computer algebra systems and databases. In this paper, we describe a Lean 4 formalization for certifying several of these number field invariants. Building on previous work on certifying rings of integers, we extend this certification approach to further invariants including the signature, the unit group modulo $p$-th powers, and, ultimately, the class group. We also improve discriminant certification, allowing verifications for higher-degree number fields infeasible in previous work. We introduce structures based on representations of algebraic objects suited to computation, including reusable ones for certifying ideal arithmetic. Along the way, we formalize several underlying mathematical results, for instance on real closed fields and pseudo-remainder sequences, which are of independent interest. We apply our framework to verify hundreds of entries of the $\textit{L-functions and modular forms database}$ (LMFDB) concerning the discriminant, signature, class number, and class group structure of various number fields. To this end, we wrote a SageMath script that computes the certificates and outputs Lean proofs of the corresponding statements.

infographic.key_insight: The paper formalizes a Lean 4 certification pipeline for key number-field invariants, extending trustworthy verification from rings of integers to signature, unit groups modulo p-th powers, discriminants, and class groups.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables computer algebra systems and databases to produce machine-checked proofs for arithmetic invariants, improving reliability of large-scale number-theory computations.
method: Build reusable Lean 4 structures for certified algebraic objects and ideal arithmetic.
Formalize supporting mathematics, including results on real closed fields and pseudo-remainder sequences.
Use SageMath to compute certificates and generate Lean proofs for the target invariants.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework was applied to verify hundreds of LMFDB entries covering discriminant, signature, class number, and class group structure.
infographic.watch_item: Certificate generation depends on the quality and compatibility of the SageMath-to-Lean workflow, which may limit automation for harder or larger-degree cases.
infographic.paper_title: Formally certifying number field invariants

title: On the robustness of noisy solutions in non-convex neural networks
authors: Enrico M. Malatesta, Alessandra Passalacqua, Riccardo Zecchina
abstract: Optimization in non-convex neural network models is strongly influenced by the geometry of the solution space: sparse, isolated, point-like clusters are typically algorithmically inaccessible, whereas wide and flat regions can be found efficiently despite being relatively rare. At zero temperature this picture has been formalized in binary perceptrons through the overlap gap property (OGP), which limits algorithmic access to configurations with zero training error above a critical constraint density $α_{\rm OGP}$. Here we extend this description to finite temperature, where a positive training error is allowed and statistically penalized. We first show that the frozen one-step replica-symmetry-breaking solution, dominating the zero temperature equilibrium measure, survives at any finite temperature. We furthermore derive a general criterion, based on the smoothness of the single-pattern Gibbs weight near the decision boundary, that determines when a finite-temperature relaxation of the loss removes freezing. We then extend the OGP construction to finite temperature and show that dense, algorithmically accessible regions of finite-energy configurations persist beyond $α_{\rm OGP}$, up to a threshold $α_{\rm OGP}(ε)$ that grows with the allowed training error $ε$. Finally, in the teacher-student setting, we show that these wide, finite-energy regions still retain good generalization. Using a finite energy message-passing algorithm, we demonstrate numerically that thermal noise enables effective generalization in the regime of constraint densities where both recovering the teacher and finding a zero temperature solution are computationally hard.

infographic.key_insight: Allowing a small finite training error preserves wide, algorithmically accessible solution regions in non-convex neural networks beyond the zero-temperature hard threshold, and these regions can still generalize well.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests that injecting or tolerating thermal noise can make hard training regimes more tractable without sacrificing predictive performance, offering a practical route for robust optimization in overconstrained models.
method: Extend the zero-temperature overlap gap property (OGP) to finite temperature with a positive loss tolerance.
Analyze freezing via a criterion based on smoothness of the single-pattern Gibbs weight near the decision boundary.
Use a finite-energy message-passing algorithm to test the predicted accessible regimes numerically.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical derivations plus numerical message-passing experiments showing that thermal noise enables effective generalization in regimes where zero-temperature solutions and teacher recovery are computationally hard.
infographic.watch_item: The finite-temperature gains depend on the allowed error level and model assumptions, so the method may not transfer directly to architectures or loss functions that do not satisfy the smoothness/mean-field conditions.
infographic.paper_title: On the robustness of noisy solutions in non-convex neural networks
